e.t: This word is the personal name “Aaron.” It identifies Aaron as a specific biblical person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. As a proper name, its meaning is primarily identifying: it points to the same individual wherever it appears in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings. The name occurs 364 times in the LXX corpus, especially in Exodus, Leviticus, and Numbers, where Aaron is frequently mentioned. Its precise significance in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This verb means “ripen”: it describes the process of becoming ripe. As a verb, it points to an action or change rather than a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 2:3. The available information identifies its basic meaning clearly, while the verse’s particular force must be understood from the surrounding passage.

This word describes something “wrought in chain manner”—made with linked parts resembling chainwork. It can function as an adjective describing an object or as a noun referring to such chainwork. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including descriptions of items connected with clothing, armor, or crafted objects. Its central idea is not merely that something is made, but that its construction has a linked, chain-like pattern.

Amessai is a proper name identifying a person in the Greek Old Testament. It is rendered as “Amessai” and also associated with the form “Amesse.” The name appears 13 times across 10 verses, mostly in 2 Samuel, with single occurrences in 1 Kings and Nehemiah. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its basic meaning is the identification of the individual who bears it; the surrounding verse is needed to understand that person’s particular role or action.

This Greek verb means “give up.” It describes the act of surrendering or handing something over rather than keeping or retaining it. As a verb, it expresses an action performed by someone toward an object or person. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, both in deuterocanonical writings: once in Sirach and once in 2 Maccabees. The precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and subject, but the central idea remains giving up or handing over.

This Greek LXX verb means “re-persuade” or “seduce”: it describes trying to influence someone again or draw that person away through persuasion. As a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. It occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in two verses spanning Jeremiah and 1 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central idea is renewed persuasion that may become enticement.

This Greek LXX verb means “refresh”: to restore someone’s strength, comfort, or renewed energy. It describes relief after weariness rather than merely a change of surroundings. The word appears six times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, including passages from Exodus, Samuel, Psalms, and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on who or what receives the refreshing, but its central idea remains renewed strength or relief.

This word means “resist”: to oppose or stand against someone or something. It is a verb describing active opposition rather than simple disagreement or withdrawal. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears 65 times, showing that it can describe resistance in varied situations and relationships. Its basic sense remains the act of standing against an opposing force, person, or claim. The surrounding sentence determines who or what is being resisted and how strongly the action is expressed.

This adverb means “unchangeably”: it describes something done or remaining without alteration. It points to steadiness or fixedness rather than a shifting, revised, or modified condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Esther 3:13. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its basic meaning is that the matter remains the same and is not changed.

This Greek LXX verb means “press from behind.” It describes pushing or crowding against someone or something from the rear, emphasizing pressure applied from behind rather than simply touching or approaching. The word occurs once in the Greek Old Testament translation, in Numbers 22:25. Because it is a verb, it expresses an action rather than a person, object, or quality. Its precise force in that verse is understood from the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX noun means “divorce,” referring to the formal ending of a marriage. It appears four times in the Old Testament Greek corpus, in passages from Deuteronomy, Isaiah, and Jeremiah. The word names the document or legal reality associated with a marital separation, rather than describing an emotion or a general departure. Its exact force in any one verse is understood from the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “cut the throat of.” It describes the act of killing someone or an animal by cutting the throat. The word is an action term, focusing on the physical act itself rather than on the person performing it or the surrounding circumstances. It occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 2:19. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, which are not included here.

This noun refers to the head of a family—the person recognized as its family leader or chief representative. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, so it is a specific term rather than a frequently repeated description. Its meaning points to family leadership and recognized responsibility within a household or larger family group. The word appears in Joshua 21:1 and Daniel 3:94, but the surrounding verse text is needed to explain each passage’s particular use.

This Greek LXX word is a proper name given as “Asōthitēs; Asothitis.” It functions as a specific designation rather than a general description or action word. The form appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, at 2 Samuel 23:27. Without the verse text and surrounding context, its precise referent cannot be described further, but its lexical role is clear: it identifies a particular named designation in that passage.

This verb means “unlucky”: it describes a person or situation that does not meet with good fortune or favorable results. As a verb, it expresses experiencing bad luck rather than merely naming an unfortunate circumstance. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Proverbs 34:10. No verse text is available, so its precise force there must be understood from the surrounding passage.

Bathrephan, also rendered Vathrefan, is a proper name referring to a person or family name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs once in the Greek LXX, in 1 Chronicles 4:12. The available information identifies the name but does not provide an ordinary descriptive meaning, role, or etymology. Therefore, it is best understood simply as a personal name preserved in this genealogical record, rather than as a word expressing an action, quality, or idea.

Baithanan is a proper name, also given as “Vethanan.” The name appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Kings 4:9. Because the available lexical information identifies the word by these name forms rather than by a descriptive definition, its ordinary meaning is its function as a specific name. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain whom or what the name identifies in that passage.

Bariai, also rendered Varie, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a specific named entity rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name occurs once in the Greek LXX, in Numbers 26:28. Without the surrounding verse text, its particular referent cannot be described more precisely, but its basic meaning is the name itself: Bariai or Varie.

This word means “hurt” or “harm,” referring to injury, damage, or something that causes loss. It is a noun, so it names the harmful result or effect rather than describing an action itself. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Wisdom 11:19. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic sense remains harm or injury.

This word means “ox goad” or “pointed stick,” a sharp implement used to direct or urge an ox. It is a noun naming a physical tool rather than an action or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Ecclesiastes 12:11. The image belongs to the ordinary world of guiding animals with a pointed staff, while its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This Greek Old Testament noun means “locust,” referring to the insect known for feeding on vegetation and appearing in swarms. It is used across ten occurrences in the Greek Old Testament, including passages that name locusts among creatures or describe them as part of agricultural devastation. The word therefore identifies a particular insect rather than expressing an action or quality. Its precise force in any individual verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains consistent: a locust.

This noun means “valley,” referring to a low area of land between hills or elevated ground. It is used in the Greek Old Testament to identify geographical places and regions. The word occurs 40 times in the Greek Old Testament, with many occurrences in Joshua, where named locations help describe Israel’s movements and battles. Its basic sense remains a physical valley or lowland; the surrounding passage determines which particular place is intended.

This word means “birth,” referring to the event or process by which a person comes into life. It is a noun, so it names the beginning of a person’s earthly life rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Leviticus and Esther. Its precise emphasis in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but its central meaning remains the beginning of life through birth.

Golam is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is given as “Gōlam; Golam.” This name occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, in 1 Chronicles 1:40. Because the surrounding verse text is not available here, its precise role in that genealogy cannot be explained further, but its lexical function is clear: it identifies a person.

This noun means “dialect,” referring to a distinct way of speaking or a particular language variety. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in Esther 9:26 and once in Daniel 1:4. Those references confirm its limited distribution in this corpus, while the word’s basic sense remains a language or speech form associated with a particular people or setting. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain its precise use in either passage.

This verb means “deceive utterly”: to act in a way that completely misleads another person. It describes deliberate deception rather than a simple mistake or misunderstanding. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs three times, each in a different verse. Its use spans 2 Kings, 1 Maccabees, and 3 Maccabees, so the word names a clear action wherever it appears, while the surrounding verse determines who deceives whom.

This noun refers to the moon in its full state—“fullness of the moon.” It names the moon’s fullness rather than describing a person, action, or character. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in Sirach 39:12. The word’s basic meaning is therefore specific and concrete: the moon when it is full. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, which is not included here.

This adjective means “Hebrew.” It identifies something as belonging to or associated with the Hebrew people or their language. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it appears twice, both times in 4 Maccabees. The word’s basic role is descriptive: it marks a person, language, or related matter as Hebrew rather than naming a separate action or quality. Its precise force in a particular sentence depends on the surrounding words, but its central meaning remains a connection with what is Hebrew.

This verb means “cut.” It describes an action performed on something, rather than naming an object, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs four times, all in 1 Kings 6, across three verses. The word’s precise object and significance depend on the sentence in which it appears, but its central idea remains the act of cutting. It is therefore best understood as an action word expressing “cut” in its immediate context.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “disrobe” or “take off,” describing the act of removing clothing or another covering. It can refer to one person removing garments from himself or to clothing being taken off another person, depending on the sentence. The word occurs 30 times in the Greek Old Testament, including the Greek translations of the Deuterocanonical books. Its basic idea remains physical removal: something worn or covering the body is taken away. The precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding context.

This Greek LXX word means “sixteen.” It is an indeclinable number word, used to identify a quantity rather than a person, action, or quality. It occurs eight times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this corpus, appearing in Numbers, Kings, and Chronicles. Its meaning remains straightforward wherever it occurs: it names the number sixteen. The surrounding verse determines what is being counted, but the word itself contributes only this numerical value.

This verb means “make a detour”: to leave the direct route and go by a different way. It describes an action rather than a person, place, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 15:3. Since the word is tied to changing one’s route, the surrounding verse is needed to identify the exact path or direction involved there.

Eliphalath is a proper name—the personal name of an individual in the Greek Old Testament. It is not presented here as a common word describing an action, quality, or object, but as a name used to identify a person. The name appears twice in the Greek Old Testament, both times in the same verse, 2 Samuel 5:16. Since the available information does not include that verse’s wording or surrounding passage, its normal meaning is simply the personal designation Eliphalath. The alternate form Elifalath is another rendering of the same name.

Elnathan is a personal name used to identify an individual, rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times across three verses, appearing in Ezra and Jeremiah. Its meaning here is therefore the name “Elnathan”; the particular person identified depends on the surrounding passage. The name is preserved consistently as “Elnathan” in the available English rendering.

This Greek LXX verb describes becoming agitated or harassing someone. It expresses troubled, forceful agitation rather than calm speech or ordinary activity. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament text, in Daniel 11:30. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains the expression of agitation or harassment directed toward someone.

This Greek LXX noun means a “pledge”: something offered or held as assurance of a commitment or obligation. It refers to what accompanies a promise or debt, rather than describing an action. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs twice: once in Exodus 22:25 and once in Ezekiel 33:15. The surrounding verse text is needed to explain how the pledge functions in either passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “direct” or “enjoin”: to give someone a command, instruction, or charge that calls for obedience. It describes authoritative direction rather than a casual suggestion. The word appears 401 times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, showing its regular use for commands given by God or by human authorities. Its precise force in a particular passage depends on who gives the instruction and what response the surrounding context requires.

This noun means contempt or scorn: an attitude that treats someone or something as unworthy of respect. It describes rejection or disdain rather than simple disagreement or dislike. In the Greek Old Testament, the word appears 11 times, mostly in the Psalms, and also in 1 Samuel, 1 Maccabees, and Song of Songs. Its basic sense remains the same across these occurrences: contempt expressed toward a person, people, or valued thing. The surrounding verse determines exactly who is being scorned and how that attitude is expressed.

This verb means to irrigate or refresh. It describes supplying moisture that renews or restores something, whether by watering it or bringing needed relief. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 1:29. The exact force of the word in that verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central sense is the giving of moisture or refreshment. It is an action word: something or someone causes another thing to become refreshed or supplied with what it needs.

This Greek LXX adjective describes something painful or toilsome—marked by hardship, strain, or difficulty. It can characterize an experience, condition, or undertaking that requires endurance rather than ease. The word occurs twice in the Greek LXX corpus, once in Sirach and once in 3 Maccabees. Its basic force remains focused on what is burdensome or difficult, while the surrounding sentence determines whether the emphasis falls more on pain, effort, or the demanding nature of a situation.

This Greek LXX noun can mean “awareness” or “insurrection.” It may describe being conscious of something or informed about it, or it may name an uprising against authority. The sentence determines which sense is intended. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Numbers. The surrounding verse text is needed to identify whether each occurrence refers to awareness or rebellion.

This verb means to state or mention something. It describes expressing information or a point in words, rather than naming an object or person as a noun would. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, so its basic sense is clear, but its precise force in either passage must come from the surrounding verse. It is a verb for an act of saying or mentioning.

This word describes doing something nobly or bravely, with honorable courage and worthy conduct. As an adverb, it tells how an action is carried out rather than naming a person, thing, or quality by itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs six times, in 2 Maccabees and 4 Maccabees. Its central sense is the manner of acting: conduct marked by nobility, courage, or both, depending on the sentence. The surrounding verse determines which aspect is most prominent.

This adjective describes something that has considerable width or spans broadly from side to side. Its central meaning is “wide; broad,” referring to physical dimensions rather than an action or feeling. In the Greek Old Testament represented here, it occurs three times, all in Exodus 38. The English renderings “wide” and “broad” express the same basic idea. The precise force in any one verse comes from the object being measured or described.

This verb describes being steady or favourable. It can characterize a condition that is settled, stable, or positively disposed, depending on the sentence in which it appears. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs three times, in 2 Maccabees and 3 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on steadiness or a favourable state, while the surrounding context determines whether the word emphasizes stability or a positive disposition.

Ēzir, also rendered Izir, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. It identifies an individual in the Greek Old Testament and appears once, in Nehemiah 10:21. Since the available lexical information gives the name itself but no further definition, its ordinary significance is simply the person identified by that name. The surrounding verse would be needed to explain that individual’s role in the passage.

Tharabaam is a proper name, also rendered “Tharavaam.” It identifies a specific named entity in the Greek Old Testament rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. The name appears once in the LXX corpus, in Joshua 15:61. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding passage, its precise referent and significance must be understood from that passage’s context.

gl: one who wills; one who wishes
d: one who wills; one who wishes

e.t: This LXX Greek word describes one who wills or wishes—someone characterized by a willing or wishing purpose. As a noun, it can refer to such a person; as an adjective, it describes someone or something marked by willingness or desire. It occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, including both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books, so its normal sense is focused and specific rather than a broad, frequently repeated term.

This noun means “ministry,” referring to service or work carried out for others. It names an activity of serving rather than a person who serves. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears six times, including passages in Genesis, Esther, and Joel. Its precise emphasis in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its central sense remains ministry or service. The word is found across these Old Testament books rather than being limited to one kind of setting.

This Greek word means to make a confused noise or to chatter. It describes speech or sound that is noisy, disordered, or lacking clear, purposeful communication. As a verb, it expresses the action of producing such chatter rather than naming the sound itself. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings, including once in Job and twice in 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any one verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

Iasoub, also rendered Iasuv, is a proper name used for people in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. The name occurs five times in the Greek LXX, appearing once each in Genesis, Numbers, 1 Chronicles, Ezra, and Isaiah. Its precise reference depends on the person named in each passage, but the word itself functions as a personal name throughout this corpus.

Ilouthōth is a proper name, preserved in English as “Iluthoth.” It identifies a specific named referent rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 15:34. The available wording does not provide an English meaning beyond the name itself, so its precise referent must be understood from the surrounding passage. This is an LXX name and should not be treated as a Greek New Testament vocabulary term.

This adjective describes something connected with horses or cavalry. It can refer to equestrian matters, especially people or forces associated with mounted service. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs twice, once in 1 Maccabees and once in 3 Maccabees. Its precise sense in either passage depends on the noun or situation it describes, but its central idea remains horse-related or cavalry-related rather than referring to ordinary travel or movement.

Isemiēl, also rendered Isemil, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. This name occurs twice in the Greek text, both within 1 Chronicles 2:31. The available information establishes the name and its use as a proper noun, but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning or etymology. Its precise significance in that passage depends on the surrounding genealogical context.

This verb means to do bad—to act wrongly or cause harm. It describes harmful or wrongful action rather than merely referring to a bad condition. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs 27 times, showing a repeated biblical way of expressing the doing of evil or injury. Its exact force in any passage depends on who is acting and what is being done, but the central idea remains active wrongdoing or harmful conduct.

Karana is a proper name, functioning as a distinctive personal or place name rather than a general description or action. Its recorded meaning is simply “Karana,” so no broader definition is established here. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at Joshua 17:9. The name’s specific referent cannot be identified from the word record alone because the verse text and surrounding context are not included.

This adjective means “of walnut,” describing something made from, belonging to, or associated with a walnut tree or its wood. It identifies the material or kind of object being mentioned rather than expressing an action or emotion. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Genesis 30:37 and Jeremiah 1:11. Its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding wording, but its basic meaning remains a reference to walnut.

This verb means to hurt greatly or to damage something or someone. It describes causing serious harm rather than merely touching, troubling, or inconveniencing. In the Greek Old Testament translation, it occurs once, in 3 Maccabees 7:8. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the precise object of the harm must be understood from that passage. Its basic sense remains the action of inflicting substantial injury or damage.

This Greek LXX verb means “deactivate; fade.” It describes something being made inactive or becoming less effective and distinct. As a verb, it expresses a change or action rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs four times, all in Ezra, so its recorded use is concentrated in that book. The exact force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage.

This LXX noun means “bees-wax,” the wax produced by bees. It refers to a physical substance rather than an action, quality, or person. The word occurs six times in the Greek Old Testament represented by this LXX corpus, appearing in Psalms, Isaiah, and Micah. Its basic meaning remains consistent wherever it occurs, while the surrounding verse determines how the substance is being used in the sentence. The word is found in Psalms 21:15, 57:9, 67:3, and 96:5, as well as Isaiah 64:1 and Micah 1:4.

“Invited” means called or welcomed to take part in something. As an adjective, this word describes a person or group that has been summoned or given an invitation. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 19 times, beginning in Exodus and continuing through 3 Maccabees. Its precise force—whether referring to people gathered for a holy observance or to others summoned for a purpose—depends on the surrounding sentence. The word emphasizes being called to participate, not merely being present.

This verb means to “have dominion,” expressing authority or ruling power over someone or something. It focuses on the exercise of control, whether by a person, ruler, or other power. The word occurs 56 times in the Greek Old Testament corpus, showing that it is used broadly for situations involving authority and strength. The surrounding verse determines who exercises this dominion and what is under it, while the word itself points to the central idea of ruling power.

This noun means “creator,” referring to the one who brings something into being. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it is used seven times, consistently with that central sense. The word can therefore identify God as the maker of creation, while its exact emphasis in any passage depends on the surrounding context. Its occurrences appear in 2 Samuel, Sirach, 2 Maccabees, and 4 Maccabees, showing its use across several writings in this corpus.

This noun means a “stone-cutter,” a person whose work involves cutting and preparing stone. It refers to a skilled worker rather than to the stone itself. In the Greek LXX, the word occurs four times, in passages connected with organized building and repair work. Its basic meaning remains focused on the worker’s trade, while the surrounding verse determines the particular construction task being discussed.

This word means “lamp”: a noun naming an object that gives light. In the Greek LXX, it occurs 45 times, so it is a recurring ordinary term rather than a rare name or technical label. Its occurrences span the Old Testament portion of the LXX and a small number of deuterocanonical passages. References include Exodus and Numbers, while the central lexical meaning remains simply “lamp.”

Madōn, also rendered Mathon, is a proper name rather than a word describing an idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, in 2 Samuel 21:20 and Ezekiel 29:18. The supplied lexical information preserves these two name forms but does not identify the person or place to whom the name belongs. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding passage, while its basic function is simply to designate someone or something by name.

This proper name refers to Megeddo, also rendered “Meyeththo,” a place-name in the Greek Old Testament. It is not a descriptive word or action but the name of a specific location. In this Greek Old Testament corpus, it occurs once, at Judges 5:19. The name itself identifies the place; understanding what occurs there requires reading the surrounding verse and passage rather than assigning extra meaning to the name.

This Greek LXX verb means “find fault”: to point out a fault or express criticism toward someone or something. It describes an act of blaming rather than simply noticing a weakness. The word occurs three times in the Greek LXX corpus, in Sirach and 2 Maccabees. Its exact force in any one passage depends on what is being criticized and why, so the surrounding verse supplies the particular emphasis. It is a verb describing the action of finding fault.

gl: being in part the cause of
d: being in part the cause of

e.t: This adjective describes someone or something that is “being in part the cause of” an outcome. It points to partial responsibility or contribution, rather than saying that the person or thing is the sole cause. The word appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Esther 8:12. Its precise force in that occurrence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic meaning identifies a contributing cause or party. It functions as a descriptive word applied to a person or thing connected with producing a result.

This LXX noun means “disturbance,” referring to a condition of disruption or unrest. It names something that unsettles what would otherwise be calm or orderly. The word occurs seven times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical books, including Psalms, Jonah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and the situation being described.

“Secretly” describes an action done out of public view or without others knowing. As an adverb, it tells how an action is carried out, rather than naming a person, object, or action itself. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, this word occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 3:10. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding verse text, which is not included here.

Naaran is a proper name, rendered as “Naaran.” It functions as a specific identifying name rather than a common word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX) represented here, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:28. Because the surrounding verse text is not provided, its precise referent cannot be identified further here; the lexical meaning itself is the name Naaran.

Nisan is the name of a month. As a proper name, it identifies that month rather than describing an action, quality, or person. In the Greek Old Testament corpus, it appears once, in Nehemiah 2:1. The word’s basic meaning is therefore simply the month-name Nisan; its significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, which is not included here.

This word means to embezzle—to take or keep money or property entrusted to you instead of using it as intended. As a verb, it describes dishonest appropriation rather than an ordinary act of taking. In the Greek Old Testament and Deuterocanonical material represented here, it occurs twice, once in Joshua and once in 2 Maccabees. The precise force in either verse depends on its surrounding context.

This noun means “drowsiness; dozing”—a state of becoming sleepy or lightly falling asleep. It describes reduced alertness rather than deep, settled sleep. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs four times, including passages in Psalms, Jeremiah, Daniel, and Sirach. The surrounding verse determines whether the word emphasizes ordinary tiredness, the onset of sleep, or a person’s lack of wakefulness.

This Greek verb means “found as a colony”: to establish a settlement or community in a place. It describes the act of planting people together in an organized habitation, rather than merely visiting or living somewhere temporarily. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs three times—once in Job and twice in Sirach. Its exact force in any particular passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

This noun refers to a kind of onyx, a gemstone or ornamental stone. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears three times: twice in Exodus and once in Ezekiel. Its references place it among descriptions of valuable stones, but the available material does not establish a more precise identification of the stone or add a distinct symbolic meaning. The word belongs to the Greek Old Testament and should be understood as naming a particular precious or decorative stone within those passages.

This word means “so; this way,” showing how something is done or indicating the manner being described. As an adverb, it can point back to an action, statement, or arrangement and identify it as happening in that manner. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented here, it occurs 812 times, so it is a common way of expressing manner or referring to what has just been said.

In the Greek Old Testament, this noun means “child” or “boy.” It refers to a young person and can describe someone in the ordinary circumstances of family, work, service, or community life. The word is used broadly across the Greek Old Testament and related writings, appearing 435 times, so its precise reference—such as a particular child or young male—comes from the sentence and surrounding passage. It is also found in both Old Testament and deuterocanonical books within this Greek corpus.

This verb means to counsel someone or appeal to them. It describes speaking to another person with guidance, encouragement, or a request. The central idea is direct personal address intended to help, persuade, or call for a response. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs 131 times, showing that this is a broadly used word for addressing people in these ways. Its exact force in a particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

This Greek LXX verb means “run by.” It describes the action of running past, alongside, or onward in relation to something or someone. As a verb, it expresses movement rather than naming a person, place, or object. The word occurs 16 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek biblical books represented here, with occurrences from 1 Samuel through 3 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding sentence, but its central idea remains movement expressed as running by.

This adjective describes someone who is needy—lacking sufficient means or resources. It identifies a condition of need rather than naming a person, place, or action. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, appearing once in Exodus and twice in Proverbs. Its basic sense remains focused on poverty or material need; the surrounding verse determines how that need is being addressed or described.

This Greek Old Testament verb means “purify completely” or “purge”—to remove what makes something unclean or impure. It describes thorough cleansing rather than a partial cleaning. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish Scripture corpus represented here, so it is uncommon but clear in its basic sense. Its exact force in any passage depends on what is being cleansed and the surrounding sentence.
